newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa trade data boosted by Botswana diamonds.
newsitem.headline: South Africa trade data boosted by Botswana diamonds.

text.p: The inclusion of proceeds from Botswana diamond exports appeared to have been the main reason for the sharp increase in South Africa's trade surplus in October, economists said on Monday.

According to the South African Revenue Services (SARS), the trade surplus rocketed 484.7 percent in October to a 3.9 billion surplus -- far exceeding economists' most optimistic forecasts of a 1.2 billion rand surplus.

The cumulative surplus for the year to October nearly doubled to 8.16 billion rand from 4.26 billion rand in September and was nearly four times the cumulative surplus of 2.16 billion rand in the same period last year.
No officials at SARS were available for comment on the data, which economists have in the past slated as erratic and unreliable.

However, a source involved in drawing up the data said Botswana diamond exports had contributed a large amount to the final figure. "There was a substantial amount of Botswana diamonds included in the figure," he said. "It was not more than two billion rand."
South African trade statistics include data from Botswana, Lesotho, Namibia and Swaziland.
The precious and semi-precious stones category of the statistics show exports rose to 5.8 billion rand in October, a 61 percent improvement on September's 3.6 billion rand.
Economists said the inclusion of Botswana diamond export proceeds of about two billion rand would make sense, but still left the country with a healthy improvement.
"Even without them you still have a stronger surplus," Rand Merchant Bank Treasury economist Julia Roy said.
The South African Foreign Trade Organisation's Anne Moore said the 23 percent year-on-year growth in exports was encouraging.
"It clearly reflects the rand devaluation coming through but over and above that there is obviously some volume growth as well," Moore said.
She noted that sectors such as machinery and base metals, which showed 24 percent and 27 percent year-on-year growth respectively, indicated increased volumes.
Roy said the fact that the trade account remained in surplus was also positive. South Africa has now recorded a trade surplus every month since July 1996.
"We know the monthly numbers are volatile, but at least we have the trend going in the right direction," she said.
"What it means for the fourth quarter is that the current account should show an improvement on the third quarter, which augurs well for interest rates and the currency next year," Roy added.

The third quarter current account deficit, which is expected to come in at 2.5 billion rand from 4.6 billion rand in the second quarter, will be announced by the Reserve Bank in its quarterly bulletin on Thursday at 1500 GMT.
